intro: CPC (cost per click) tells you the average price paid for each click on an ad. Enter total spend and clicks below to get the rate.

sections.heading: How CPC is calculated
sections.body: CPC is total spend divided by clicks. Spend $500 on a campaign that gets 250 clicks and the average CPC is $500 ÷ 250 = $2.00. [Google Ads defines its own Average CPC](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/14074) the same way — total cost of clicks divided by total number of clicks — and this ratio is the common shape most auction-based ad platforms use, though the exact terminology and what gets reported (max bid, actual cost, average cost) can differ by platform. What always varies between campaigns is the price the auction settles on for each click.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: $2.00 is what this campaign paid on average for a click — some individual clicks cost more, some less, and CPC is the blended rate across all 250. It says nothing on its own about whether those clicks were worth $2.00 each; that depends on what happened after someone clicked.

sections.heading: What CPC tells you, and what it doesn't
sections.body: CPC tells you how efficiently a campaign is buying traffic — the price paid per visitor, isolated from everything that happened after the click. That makes it useful for comparing bidding strategies, ad groups, or keywords against each other on acquisition cost alone. It doesn't tell you whether that traffic was any good. A lower CPC isn't automatically a better campaign: clicks can be cheap because they're low-intent, off-target, or from an audience unlikely to ever convert, and a bidding change that cuts CPC in half can just as easily cut the [conversion rate](/calculators/cr) in half too. CPC is a cost-efficiency read on acquiring a click, not a verdict on the traffic's value — that requires looking past CPC at what the clicks actually did.

sections.heading: CPC vs. CPM vs. CPA
sections.body: These three answer different questions about the same spend. CPC is the average cost paid for an ad click — not necessarily a site visit, since a click can lead to an app, a call, or another kind of interaction depending on the ad format. [CPM](/calculators/cpm) is cost per thousand impressions — what it cost to be shown, whether anyone clicked or not. CPA is cost per defined conversion action — what it cost to get the outcome that was actually being paid for, whatever that's set to be. A campaign can carry a low CPC and a high CPA at the same time if plenty of people click but few of them convert, which is exactly why comparing bids across campaigns on CPC alone can favor the wrong one.

related.name: Conversion Rate Calculator

faq.a: CPC (cost per click) is the average amount an advertiser pays each time someone clicks an ad, calculated as total spend divided by total clicks. It's a bidding and reporting metric used across search, social and display advertising to measure how much traffic acquisition costs at the click level. CPC only covers the transaction of paying for a click — it has no visibility into what that visitor did afterward, whether they converted, or what the business ultimately made from them. On auction-based platforms like Google Ads, an account can show more than one CPC figure — a maximum bid (the most an advertiser set as willing to pay) alongside an actual or average CPC (what was really charged) — but the exact terminology and how many figures get reported varies by platform, so check what a specific dashboard's CPC field actually represents before comparing it elsewhere.

Divide total spend by total clicks: CPC = Spend ÷ Clicks. A campaign that spent $500 and received 250 clicks has a CPC of $500 ÷ 250 = $2.00. Both numbers need to cover the same campaign and date range — spend from a full month divided by clicks from only part of it produces a CPC that doesn't describe either period accurately. Most ad platforms calculate and display this automatically, so it rarely needs to be computed by hand, but the underlying formula explains why CPC moves the way it does: raising a bid to win more competitive auctions pushes the average up, while a shift toward less contested keywords or placements pulls it back down without spend or clicks necessarily changing much.

faq.q: Does a lower CPC always mean a better campaign?
faq.a: No. CPC only measures what a click cost, not what it was worth, so a lower number can reflect cheaper access to a worse audience rather than a more efficient campaign. Broadening targeting, loosening keyword match types, or shifting budget toward lower-competition placements can affect CPC and sometimes reduce it, depending on auction dynamics and how the targeting change actually plays out — but that traffic can also carry lower purchase intent or be less relevant to what's being sold, which shows up later as a weaker conversion rate. That's not a rule that lower CPC is bad either — sometimes cheaper clicks convert just as well. The point is that CPC by itself can't tell the difference, so a change in CPC needs to be read alongside conversion rate or cost per acquisition before deciding whether it actually helped.

There's no universal good CPC — it depends on the platform, the auction's competitiveness, the audience being targeted, the geography, and where the ad is placed, all of which shift what a click costs before performance even enters the picture. A CPC that looks high for one keyword or industry can be entirely normal for another with more competitive bidding or higher customer value. Rather than comparing against a published average, CPC is most useful measured against your own account's history in the same campaign type, or against what a click needs to cost for the resulting conversions to be worth acquiring — a number your own margins and conversion rate determine, not a benchmark pulled from somewhere else.
